title: AI Vendor Risk Assessment Categories
status: Proposed extension of the CoSAI Shared Responsibility Framework; not part of CoSAI SRF v1.0; not an endorsement of any named vendor; not legal advice.
description: Seven AI vendor categories mapped to the CoSAI SRF. Each category states the SRF layers and operating models it touches, the responsibilities the vendor owns versus those the customer keeps, the attestation baseline, and the evidence to demand before signing. Inventory, tiering, and contracting for all seven categories sit at L1. L5 is the model-artifact chain. Includes a three-tier risk model, cross-cutting AI risks to check on every vendor, and a reference for what each attestation actually proves.

risk_tiers.label: Critical
risk_tiers.triggers: Regulated or highly sensitive data; autonomous actions on your systems; deep platform or model access (L4 or L5).
risk_tiers.assessment_depth: Full assessment, all evidence asks, contractual SRF responsibility matrix, continuous evidence rather than point-in-time, named incident path.

risk_tiers.label: Elevated
risk_tiers.triggers: Internal business data; human-in-the-loop; application-layer AI features (L3).
risk_tiers.assessment_depth: Core attestations plus the AI-specific asks for the category, data-use and sub-processor disclosure, admin controls review.

risk_tiers.label: Standard
risk_tiers.triggers: Low-sensitivity data; bounded scope; no autonomy; no training on your data.
risk_tiers.assessment_depth: Baseline attestation (SOC 2 or ISO 27001), acceptable use terms, data-retention and deletion commitment.

tiering_note: Depth of assessment should track the risk a vendor introduces, not the size of the contract. Score each vendor on three axes: sensitivity of data touched, autonomy exercised, and depth reached into the SRF stack. The highest of the three sets the tier.

categories.title: Core AI platform & infrastructure
categories.summary: Cloud AI services, MLOps pipelines, model hosting, GPU infrastructure.
categories.vendor_accountable_for: Tenant isolation, platform and infrastructure security, encryption services, availability, and the platform telemetry it exposes.
categories.customer_accountable_for: Workload and key configuration, data classification, identity and access, app-layer controls, and deciding which AI events and logs you collect.

risk_areas.evidence: Architecture diagrams showing how one customer is prevented from reaching another's data, and where data resides.

risk_areas.risk_area: Encryption at rest and in transit
risk_areas.evidence: Key-management description and bring-your-own-key options.
Current attestation reports under NDA, with scope and exceptions.
Which AI events the platform generates, how models are monitored, and which logs you are expected to collect.
A responsibility matrix that states who owns what, plus the adversarial or bias testing the platform expects you to run.

categories.title: Pre-trained model & algorithm providers
categories.summary: Foundation and domain-specific models reached by API: LLMs, vision, and speech models.
categories.vendor_accountable_for: Training and model integrity, safety tuning, model and system cards, API security, and not training on your prompts where contracted.
categories.customer_accountable_for: Use-case risk classification, prompt and output handling, application guardrails, and human oversight of model output.

risk_areas.evidence: Third-party benchmark certification and robustness metrics against adversarial attacks and jailbreaks.
Proof of data opt-out (GDPR, CCPA) and a list of third-party datasets used.
System and model cards covering intended use, limits, and evaluation.
License and acceptable-use terms, plus an IP indemnity clause for model output.
Mapping of the model to EU AI Act risk categories and proof that prompts are not used for training.
Model provenance and signing, weight-integrity controls, and a vulnerability disclosure process.

categories.title: AI-enabled SaaS applications
categories.summary: SaaS products with embedded AI features: copilots, assistants, and AI inside tools you already buy. The category most companies actually procure.
categories.vendor_accountable_for: Application logic, in-app guardrails, output filtering, feature-level access control, and the foundation models it selects underneath.
categories.customer_accountable_for: What data you feed the app, user permissions, acceptable use, and monitoring AI output for your own context and accuracy.

risk_areas.evidence: Which foundation models and sub-processors power the feature, and the data flow to each.
Input and output filtering, indirect prompt-injection defenses, and jailbreak test results.
Contractual proof that tenant data is not used to train shared models.
Admin controls to disable AI features and audit logs of AI actions taken in your tenant.
Isolation evidence and data-residency options.

categories.title: Agentic AI & autonomous systems
categories.summary: Autonomous agents, tool-using copilots, workflow automation, and the tool and connector ecosystems (for example MCP servers) that agents act through.
categories.vendor_accountable_for: The agent runtime, tool and permission scoping, guardrail enforcement, action logging, and the autonomy and override controls it exposes.
categories.customer_accountable_for: Which tools and scopes you grant, how you configure human override and approval gates, and the blast-radius limits you set.

risk_areas.evidence: The autonomy levels (L0 to L5) and override tiers (T1 to T5) the product supports, and its default settings.
The permission model, scope limits, and the ability to require human approval per action class.
Detection of guardrail bypass, runtime integrity verification, and a complete action audit trail.
Rate limits, spend caps, rollback, and a documented kill-switch.
Defenses for the case where an agent reads untrusted content or tool output and acts on it.

categories.title: Data, labeling & retrieval services
categories.summary: Managed labeling, RLHF, and crowdsourcing platforms, plus retrieval and vector-data providers that feed RAG systems.
categories.vendor_accountable_for: Workforce vetting, confidential-data controls, annotation quality, retrieval-index security, and secure deletion on request.
categories.customer_accountable_for: Classifying data before you share it, defining the retention policy, and accepting the quality thresholds you contract to.

risk_areas.evidence: Which roles or regions are exempt from screening, and the re-screening cadence for gig workers and contractors.
DLP evidence, GeoIP and embargo restrictions, and penetration-test results for any contractor-provided VDI.
QA methodology documentation and the prior-quarter metrics dashboard.
Sub-processor list with change control, a data-flow diagram with geographies, audit results, and opt-out options.
Whether you can define the retention policy, plus certificates of data deletion or destruction.
Access controls on the vector store, data-poisoning defenses, and tenant isolation of embeddings.

categories.title: AI consulting & professional services
categories.summary: Strategy, custom model development, and system integration.
categories.srf_layers_note: Cross-layer; anchored at L1 AI Business & Usage.
categories.vendor_accountable_for: Secure development practice, deliverable quality, the firm's own security posture, and clean exit from your environment.
categories.customer_accountable_for: Scope definition, environment-access boundaries, IP terms, and acceptance criteria for what the engagement produces.

risk_areas.evidence: Examples of AI KPI dashboards and prior-project scorecards.
Restricted data and system-access requirements such as VPN, VDI, Jupyter Hub, and IDE.

risk_areas.risk_area: Ownership of code and models produced
risk_areas.evidence: Contracts addressing IP or joint ownership, plus SBOM and AIBOM breakdowns of what was delivered.
Third-party attestation results for the consulting firm itself.
Destruction certificates, the process for sanitizing IDE and repos (Jira, Confluence, Git), and wiping developer workstations and VDI caches.

categories.title: Software, VARs & distributors
categories.summary: Bundled AI software, marketplace sellers, and OEM integrators that resell or repackage AI built by someone else.
categories.vendor_accountable_for: Passing through the OEM's controls without weakening them, delivering patches, and providing support and escalation.
categories.customer_accountable_for: Validating the OEM behind the reseller and holding both to the contract terms and the downstream supply chain.

risk_areas.evidence: Model, dataset, and tool patch schedule, plus an end-of-life matrix by product.
A controls-hardening benchmark and a contract clause ensuring the vendor cannot weaken security settings over time.
Named contacts and numbers, and the incident-response process.
Current sub-provider inventory with geographic locations and data roles, audit results, and opt-out options.
Licensing and warranty coverage, with legal sign-off.

cross_cutting_risks.title: Prompt injection, direct and indirect
cross_cutting_risks.description: Whether the vendor defends against malicious instructions in user input and in content the system retrieves or a tool returns.

cross_cutting_risks.title: Model and weight supply chain
cross_cutting_risks.description: Provenance, signing, and poisoning or backdoor defenses for models and weights. Ask for an AIBOM alongside the SBOM.

cross_cutting_risks.title: Training-data provenance and IP
cross_cutting_risks.description: What the model was trained on, opt-out handling, and indemnity for IP claims arising from output.

cross_cutting_risks.title: Data residency and sub-processors
cross_cutting_risks.description: Where data and inference run, the full sub-processor chain, and notice and opt-out on changes.

cross_cutting_risks.title: Continuous vs point-in-time evidence
cross_cutting_risks.description: Whether the vendor can show controls operating over time, not just a once-a-year attestation snapshot.

cross_cutting_risks.title: Versioning and decommissioning
cross_cutting_risks.description: How model and feature versions are tracked, notified, deprecated, and rolled back without breaking your controls.

cross_cutting_risks.title: Liability for AI-generated harm
cross_cutting_risks.description: Contractual allocation of liability when model output causes financial, legal, or safety harm.

cross_cutting_risks.title: AI management system maturity
cross_cutting_risks.description: Whether the vendor runs a governed AI program. ISO 42001 certification and a NIST AI RMF profile are the signals.

attestation_reference.covers: Operating effectiveness of security, availability, and confidentiality controls over a period.
attestation_reference.does_not_cover: AI-specific risk, model behavior, bias, or autonomy.

attestation_reference.covers: A certified information security management system.
A certified AI management system: governance, risk, and lifecycle controls for AI. The AI-specific signal.
attestation_reference.does_not_cover: Point-in-time security control testing of infrastructure.

attestation_reference.covers: Quality management. Relevant to labeling and annotation accuracy.
US federal authorization for cloud services at a defined impact level.
attestation_reference.does_not_cover: AI governance beyond the underlying cloud platform.

attestation_reference.covers: A voluntary AI risk-management profile. Shows the vendor has a structured AI risk process.
attestation_reference.does_not_cover: Independent certification; it is self-applied unless audited.

attestation_reference.covers: Risk categorization and the legal obligations that follow for in-scope systems.
attestation_reference.does_not_cover: A security or quality attestation on its own.
